Outline.md
# Outline (revision 1) — story-repo

Working from: `Brief` of idea-repo (revision 2), objective `story-repo#1`. This page says **what to test and what each part of the paper says**; it never says what a result must be. Where a result decides between two stories, both are written below (§6) so nobody has to rewrite the paper's frame after the fact.

## 0. The paper in one paragraph
Evaluating an LLM on a full benchmark is costly, so we run it on n ≪ N items and predict its full score. Existing methods (anchor points, tinyBenchmarks, metabench, assessor, active acquisition) use the score matrix of *source models* to pick items and fit a *latent model* of the target; they are judged mostly on held-out models that resemble the sources. We cast the problem as **finite-population estimation of a mean of N unknown 0/1 values with a free covariate (the source matrix)**. That frame separates what the sources can buy — **variance reduction** — from what must be controlled by design — **bias**. We (i) test, on 13 binary matrices and under three target splits (interpolation, extrapolation, lineage-held-out), whether model-based predictors lose accuracy where targets differ from the sources; (ii) test whether a design-based correction (probability sampling with a positivity floor + difference/GREG estimator) repairs it and at what variance cost; (iii) measure how much the source matrix can help at all over plain stratified/balanced random sampling; (iv) examine ordering of models separately from score error. A negative or conditional answer to any of these is a result.

Working title (not final): *What do source models buy? Design-based benchmark prediction from a few items.*

## 1. Claims, evidence each needs, and the figure/table that carries it
Primary endpoint (fixed by the idea before running): **RMSE ratio to uniform random sampling at a stated n (and n/N), geometric mean over benchmarks, paired clustered bootstrap CI, per split.** Everything else is secondary.

| # | Claim (to be tested) | Evidence needed from analysis | Carried by |
|---|---|---|---|
| C0 | Setting and protocol are sound: item selection/tuning use sources only, same n for all methods, shared seeds, one subset serves all targets in a draw | Data audit (per file: N, #models, score range, binary-ness, families); leakage checks; `benchpred` cross-check | Table 1 (audit, main or appendix by venue budget); protocol Fig. 1 |
| C1 | **Comparison:** how do model-based, anchor-based and design-based methods rank by the primary endpoint under each split, over n from ~10 to a few hundred? | Tier-1 on all 13 benchmarks (uniform, stratified, source-calibrated regression, anchors, balanced selection with overfitting check, ours); Tier-2 as far as budget allows (tinyBenchmarks, metabench-style, kNN/low-rank, IRT-CAT); "not run" stated for anything not run | Fig. 2 (RMSE ratio vs n, one panel per split), Table 2 (primary endpoint, method × split, with CI and k/#families) |
| C2 | **Bias–variance:** model-based predictors show signed bias that grows away from the source range (compression toward the source mean); the difference estimator removes it and costs a stated amount of variance — or it does not | Signed error vs true score per method class, extrapolation split especially; bias/variance decomposition; λ, ε tuned on sources only; LOO-vs-naive fit bias for sampled items | Fig. 3 (signed error vs true target score), Table 3 (bias² / variance / RMSE by method) |
| C3 | **Factorial ablation:** a win is attributable to design, estimator, or their combination, not to a weak comparator | design {uniform, stratified, uncertainty-PPS, balanced, anchor medoids, IRT-CAT} × estimator {mean/Hájek, calibrated regression, model-based, difference} | Fig. 4 (heatmap, RMSE ratio, primary n; one panel per split or interp+extrap) |
| C4 | **Ceiling:** the gain over random sampling is bounded by how well sources predict the target's unseen items, and varies with benchmark | P

# Review of the plan (Outline rev 1, story-repo wiki, 05:14 UTC) against the objective and Brief rev 2

Verdict: the outline answers what the objective asks. It carries every rubric item (novelty/positioning, baselines + ablation, uncertainty, scope of conclusions, limitations), it fixes the primary endpoint before running, it writes the endings in advance (§6, including the negative one), and it keeps "extrapolation is hard" out of the claims. Each claim names its evidence and the figure that carries it. I have no objection to the story. What follows would make the plan decide its claims at a size that can decide them; items 1–4 are the ones I would fix before analysis starts.

## Fix before analysis starts
1. **Tuning must mimic the split it serves (affects C1, C2, the headline).** ε and λ are "tuned on sources only". If they are tuned on random held-out sources, they are tuned for interpolation, and the model-based/difference weighting will be wrong for the extrapolation split — either favouring the model-based predictor (λ→0) or understating the correction. For the extrapolation split, tune on a *nested* extrapolation split inside the source set (hold out the strongest sources, fit on the rest); for lineage-held-out, hold out source families. State this in §4/§5.1 and ask analysis to report sensitivity of the primary endpoint to λ, ε. Otherwise a reviewer can say C2 was decided by how the hyperparameters were tuned.
2. **C2's bias/variance accounting needs the right unit (Fig. 3, Table 3).** Bias of a design-based estimator is defined over subset draws *for a fixed target*; the one-subset-per-draw-for-all-targets protocol is fine, but bias and variance must be computed per target over draws first (many draws, ≥100 where cheap), then summarised across targets, with the Monte Carlo standard error of the per-target bias shown. Pooling across targets and draws mixes target heterogeneity into "variance". Say so in §3 and put it in the ask to analysis (§4).
3. **A stated minimum for Tier 2 (the open point in §8).** What a reviewer would require at minimum: tinyBenchmarks (anchors+IRT; named in the objective's starter literature and the usual comparator) and a kNN/low-rank source-model baseline on **all 13** files, since these are cheap; metabench-style and IRT-CAT may be restricted to the larger files if cost forces it, but the restriction must be stated by cost, not chosen after seeing results. The proposal "7 OLL + 3 HELM" does not say which 3 HELM or why; replace by a rule (cost-based, fixed in advance). Tier 3 "not run" is acceptable provided the limitations section says it plainly.
4. **C4 as written can be circular or merely mechanical (Fig. 5).** "Oracle-ish predictor quality vs best achievable RMSE ratio, one point per benchmark × split" correlates two quantities tied by the variance formula, over ~39 non-independent points (same models across splits and across HELM benchmarks). Stronger: define predictor quality as the *source-only* predictor's residual-variance fraction on held-out targets' full item vectors (target answers not used), derive the RMSE ratio the difference estimator should achieve from it (design variance formula), and show predicted vs observed ratio; deviations are the finding. Then C4 is a check of the theory, not a correlation. Also state this ceiling does not cover model-based predictors that use the target's n answers to fit latent ability (they can exceed it in interpolation).

## Should address
5. **Add one cheap analysis that answers "what do source models buy" directly: error vs number of source models M** (subsample the sources, e.g. M = 10, 30, 100, all). It is the practical question for anyone with few historical evaluations, separates C4 from "which benchmark", and costs little. Fits in Fig. 5 or an appendix figure. Same for the near-duplicate share of the sources (the family-removed variant already covers part of it).

shown.message:
I reviewed the Outline (revision 1) and posted the review to `story-repo` as issue #3.

The Outline answers what the objective asks, and I have no objection to the story. It fixes the primary endpoint before running, writes the possible endings in advance (including the negative one), and keeps "extrapolation is hard" out of the claims.

Four points should be fixed before analysis starts:
- **Tuning per split:** ε and λ should be tuned on a nested extrapolation split inside the source set, not on random held-out sources. Otherwise the extrapolation result depends on how the hyperparameters were tuned.
- **Bias and variance unit:** bias must be computed per target over subset draws first, then summarised across targets. Pooling mixes target differences into variance.
- **Tier-2 minimum:** tinyBenchmarks and a kNN/low-rank baseline should run on all 13 files, and any restriction on the rest should be a cost-based rule fixed in advance. The Outline's "7 OLL + 3 HELM" doesn't say which three HELM files or why.
- **C4 ceiling claim:** as written it ties two quantities that the variance formula already links. It should compare the predicted RMSE ratio with the observed one.

I also asked for six smaller things:
- An error-versus-number-of-source-models analysis.
- A note that IRT-CAT (adaptive item selection per target) doesn't fit the shared-subset protocol or the ordering reference.
- A primary n of 100 plus a secondary n/N, because 100 is 18% of IFEval (N≈541) but under 1% of MMLU-Pro (N≈12k).
- Costing the factorial ablation.
- Priorities under the page limit.
- A definition of the extrapolation split.

I'll review again when the Outline changes.
